name: Altmarkt
label: Altmarkt
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap: Altmarkt, Innere Altstadt, Altstadt, Dresden, Sachsen, Deutschland
notes: Home of the Striezelmarkt in December.

text.description:
Altmarkt is the old market square in the heart of Dresden's Altstadt, and it is a handy first stop for a phone photographer. The open space gives you room to step back and fit a lot into the frame. That is rare in a historic centre, where streets are often too narrow for a wide view. The buildings around the square make a natural frame, and people crossing it give a sense of scale and everyday life.

The phone icon on the map is about 65 m west of the subject. From there you can take in the whole width of the square, with its edges leading the eye into the picture. Walk around a little before you settle. Small changes in position, or crouching a bit lower, change how much sky and paving you include.

Enjoy this square as a place to take in the old town's atmosphere rather than a single landmark. Take a general view first, then step closer for details such as building fronts and street scenes. Keep your phone lens clean, as a smudge shows up badly in bright, open scenes. If the square is busy or has temporary structures, the view may look different, so be ready to adjust your position.
text.geographic_location: Altmarkt is in the Innere Altstadt, the old town centre of Dresden, in the Altstadt district.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. The centre of the square is then about 1 minute on foot to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole square in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out details on the far side.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The square then opens out in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the horizon and building edges straight. Put the square's edge or a line of paving in the lower third to lead the eye across. Wait for people to walk through the frame to add scale. If you can, hold the phone at chest height rather than eye level for a steadier, cleaner view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo to catch people moving, and use panorama only if you want the whole width of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually has fewer people, if you want an emptier square. Evening light can be pleasant, and night mode helps once it gets dark.

text.access_note: Altmarkt looks like an open public square, but check local event information before you go, as the square may be busy at times.

name: Frauenkirche
label: Frauenkirche
camera_source: Commons cluster (57 photos).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Frauenkirche, Dresden'.

text.description:
The Frauenkirche (Church of Our Lady) is a Lutheran church in the middle of Dresden, and its bell-shaped dome gave the city a distinctive silhouette. The current building is the third church on this site. The Baroque church was built between 1726 and 1743 to a design by the city architect George Bähr. It was destroyed in the bombing of February 1945, and its ruins stood for nearly half a century as a war memorial. Rebuilding began in 1994, the exterior was finished in 2004 and the church was reconsecrated on 30 October 2005. The original dome, called the 'Stone Bell', was about 67 metres high and rested on eight slender supports. The surrounding Neumarkt square was rebuilt in 2004 with its Baroque-style buildings.

It photographs well because the curved dome and the pale, weathered stonework stand out against the surrounding buildings and the sky. From the phone icon on the map you are close enough to fill the frame with the church but still far enough back to see the dome and the lower walls together. Stand still for a moment before you shoot. Square-on shots work well, and so does a slight angle that shows the curves of the walls. People walking past the front add a sense of scale, so you don't need to wait for an empty frame.
text.geographic_location: The Frauenkirche stands in Dresden's old town, in the middle of the rebuilt Neumarkt square, with the Baroque-style buildings of the square around it.
text.directions_text: Head for the Neumarkt square in the centre of Dresden. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the church and its dome together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the buildings around it. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the dome and the stonework, but keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the dome with a vertical line so the church stands straight. Leave a little sky above the dome, and include some of the square in front for scale. Try one shot at 1x and one at 0.5x with the phone held level, so the walls don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the colour of the stone, and early in the day the square is usually quieter. After dark, night mode can work if you rest your elbows on something steady.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the church itself is a place of worship and visitor site, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or entry rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Low morning or late-afternoon sun tends to bring out the colour of sandstone.
The square is usually quieter early in the morning.

name: Zwinger
label: Zwinger
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Zwinger (Dresden)'.

text.description: The Zwinger is a Baroque palace complex with gardens on the edge of Dresden's old town, designed by Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann. It began in 1709 as an orangery, garden and festival ground for Augustus the Strong, and it is still one of the city's best-known buildings. Today it is a museum complex, home to the Old Masters Picture Gallery, the Porcelain Collection and the Mathematisch-Physikalischer Salon. It photographs well because the pavilions and long galleries are decorated with balustrades, statues and vases, so almost any angle gives you rhythm and detail. The name comes from a medieval word for the strip of ground between two defensive walls, even though the palace no longer served that purpose when it was built. Gottfried Semper closed the open side towards the Elbe with the Semper Gallery, which opened in 1855. Heavy bomb damage in February 1945 was followed by rebuilding in the 1950s and 1960s. Take one wide shot to show the scale, then move in for the carved figures, the gateways and the roofline. Look out for the Kronentor, the crown gate finished in 1714, which makes a good close-up of its own. Walk a few steps between shots, because the view changes quickly.
text.geographic_location: The Zwinger lies on the north-western edge of Dresden's Innere Altstadt (inner old town). It sits right beside Theaterplatz, the Semperoper and Dresden Castle.
text.directions_text: Make for the Innere Altstadt and Theaterplatz, next to the Semperoper; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Zwinger. The Elbe terraces are roughly 200 metres to the north-east, which helps you get your bearings. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long galleries and pavilions into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a single building. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for statues, vases and the Kronentor.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there the complex lies to the south-east, so you are looking across it rather than up at one wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the long gallery rooflines with the horizontal lines so they stay straight. Keep the phone level and avoid tilting it up, or the buildings will lean inwards. Use a pavilion or a row of statues as your main subject, and leave a little sky above it. Try one wide shot and one telephoto detail from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest stone area to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the pale facades keep their detail. Leave Live Photos off unless people are moving through the scene, so you don't capture a blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the stonework and fewer people in the frame. On a dull day the carved detail still shows well.

text.access_note: The Zwinger is a museum and event complex, so access to the courtyard and the museums may vary; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is on the north-west side of the complex, so the view from there looks across the Zwinger towards the south-east.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light and fewer visitors.
The Kronentor makes a good telephoto subject, and the stone facades are pale.
Access to the courtyard and museums may vary by day or event.

name: Dresden Castle (Residenzschloss)
label: Dresden Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Augustusbrücke' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Augustusbrücke' (way/192544387): middle (352 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Dresden Castle'.

text.description:
Dresden Castle, also called the Royal Palace, is one of the oldest buildings in the city. It was the home of the electors and kings of Saxony for almost 400 years, and for part of that time of the Kings of Poland too. It began as a Romanesque keep around 1200, and the Hausmannsturm tower dates from the early 15th century. After a fire in 1701 much of it was rebuilt in the Baroque style. Most of it was left a roofless shell by the bombing of 13 February 1945, and restoration is still going on. Today it is a museum complex.

It photographs well because you see it as part of the city rather than on its own. From the phone icon on the map, on the Augustusbrücke, the castle sits in the middle of a skyline with the Frauenkirche and the Semperoper alongside it. Guides often call the bridge the classic Dresden photo spot. Walk out toward the Altstadt side and let the buildings line up in front of you.

If you want a closer, frontal picture instead, Theaterplatz shows the castle beside the Hofkirche across the square, and the Taschenberg/Sophienstraße corner is another place to try for the facade.
text.geographic_location: The castle is in Dresden's Altstadt (old town), next to the Hofkirche and Theaterplatz. The Augustusbrücke viewpoint is a short walk to its north-east.
text.directions_text: Head for the Augustusbrücke on foot. The castle lies to the south-west of the phone icon on the map. From the bridge it is about 350 m (a few minutes' walk) to the castle itself. The phone icon on the map is about 350 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the bridge, the skyline and the sky in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view of the buildings. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick the castle out of the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 350 m north-east of the subject, on Augustusbrücke (the phone icon on the map), and face south-west. From there the castle sits in the middle of a skyline with the Frauenkirche and the Semperoper alongside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the skyline level. Let the bridge railing or pavement lead the eye toward the castle. Take one wide shot of the whole skyline, then a zoomed one of the castle. If you want a frontal view instead, try Theaterplatz, where the castle stands beside the Hofkirche.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework does not turn dark. Panorama mode can work for the full skyline if you hold the phone steady and move slowly. Wait for a gap in passers-by before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or in the hour before sunset is usually kinder than harsh midday sun. Early in the day also tends to mean fewer people on the bridge.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on a public bridge, but the castle is a museum complex that is still being restored and some parts need advance booking, so check the official site before you go.

name: Semperoper
label: Semperoper
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Theaterplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Theaterplatz' (way/1415192048): middle (307 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Semperoper'.

text.description: The Semperoper is Dresden's opera house, standing on Theaterplatz close to the Elbe in the historic centre. It photographs well because the square gives you room to step back and fit the whole Neo-Renaissance front into one frame, with the panther quadriga (a chariot group with a statue of Dionysos) on top of the portal. The first opera house here, by Gottfried Semper, opened in 1841. After a fire in 1869 the citizens of Dresden asked for Semper to rebuild it. He was in exile by then, so his son Manfred built the second house to his plans, finished in 1878. The building was largely destroyed in 1945, leaving only the outer shell, and the reconstruction was completed on 13 February 1985, very close to its pre-war look. From the phone icon on the map, the King Johann monument makes a good foreground and gives a sense of scale. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. Take a few frames at different distances, then zoom in on the sculpture above the portal. If you have time, the Brühlsche Terrasse is a good second viewpoint. It is the raised promenade by the Elbe, reached by stairs from the square, and from there you see the opera with the Hofkirche and Frauenkirche in the wider view.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Dresden, on Theaterplatz near the Elbe. The Brühlsche Terrasse promenade is close by.
text.directions_text: Head to Theaterplatz in Dresden's historic centre, the square in front of the opera. The phone icon on the map is on the west side of the square, near the King Johann statue. From there the opera is to the north, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade and the King Johann monument. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the building will not fit, and keep the phone level. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the quadriga and the sculptures on the portal.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m south of the subject, in Theaterplatz (the phone icon on the map), and face north. In front of the main facade on the west side of the square near King Johann's statue. From here you see the opera's Neo-Renaissance front and the panther quadriga across the square, with the King Johann monument in the foreground. The opera is to the north of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the facade up with them. Put the statue low in the frame as a foreground and leave the quadriga near the top. Try one frame at 1x and another zoomed in on the portal. For a different view, go up to the Brühlsche Terrasse and shoot the opera from the terrace, with the Hofkirche and Frauenkirche in the wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and steady the phone against something solid, and wait for the shot to finish.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before the afternoon, when the front of the building gets its light. After dusk is good for the illuminated facade and night views.

text.access_note: Theaterplatz is an open public square; if you want to go inside the opera house, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide shots taken close to a tall building can make its vertical lines lean, so keeping the phone level helps.
Exposure may need lowering when the sky behind the building is bright.

name: Dresden Cathedral (Hofkirche)
label: Hofkirche
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brühlsche Terrasse' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Brühlsche Terrasse' (relation/3288098): middle (309 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Dresden Cathedral'.

text.description:
Dresden Cathedral, also called the Hofkirche, is the city's Catholic cathedral and one of its best-known landmarks. It was designed by Gaetano Chiaveri between 1738 and 1751 for Augustus III, the Catholic ruler of a mostly Protestant city. It was built at the same period as the Frauenkirche, and a raised walkway linked it to the castle. The church was badly damaged in February 1945 and was restored by 1962. The bridge to the castle was rebuilt in the early 21st century. Inside are a Rococo pulpit by Balthasar Permoser, an organ by Gottfried Silbermann and the crypts of the Wettin family, where the heart of Augustus the Strong is buried.

It photographs well because the tall facade and dome sit right beside the Residenzschloss and the Elbe, so one frame can hold the cathedral, the castle and the river. The phone icon on the map is on the Brühlsche Terrasse, and from there the cathedral lies to the west. Guides and photographers single this spot out for the blue hour, when the stonework stands out against a deep sky. If the terrace is busy or closed, Schlossplatz gives a close, frontal view instead.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Dresden, beside the Elbe and next to the Residenzschloss (Dresden Castle).
text.directions_text: There is no tram or railway stop right at this spot, so head for the historic centre of Dresden beside the Elbe. Walk to the cathedral, then continue east to the stairs at the river end of the Brühlsche Terrasse. The phone icon on the map is about 220 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the facade, the dome, the castle and the river together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 220 m east of the subject, on Brühlsche Terrasse (the phone icon on the map), and face west. On the stairs (Freitreppe) at the river end of the terrace, and look west. From there the cathedral's facade and dome line up with the Residenzschloss, with the Elbe in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the cathedral on one of the vertical lines, with the river along the lower third. Keep your phone level so the tall facade does not lean. If you want a different view, Schlossplatz gives a close, frontal shot with the connecting bridge, and Königsufer gives a panorama across the river that includes the Frauenkirche.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At blue hour, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the stairs or railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, just after sunset or just before sunrise.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a place of worship that allows free entry in the daytime, but the Brühlsche Terrasse and the terrace stairs may have access changes or closures, so check the official site before you go.

name: Brühl's Terrace
label: Brühl's Terrace
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Brühl's Terrace'.

text.description:
Brühl's Terrace is a long, raised promenade above the river Elbe, on the north side of the Neumarkt and the Frauenkirche. It is nicknamed "The Balcony of Europe", a name from the early 19th century. The terrace began as part of the city's fortifications, rebuilt after the Schmalkaldic War of 1546/47. It takes its name from Count Heinrich von Brühl, who was given the whole terrace in 1747. It was opened to the public in 1814, and a flight of stairs at the western end, from Castle Square (Schlossplatz), was built to reach it. The area was destroyed in February 1945 and has since been rebuilt, and it now looks very much as it did in the past.

It photographs well because several things share one frame: the stone balustrade, the river below, and a line of grand buildings including the Academy of Fine Arts and the Albertinum, with statues along the way. Look for small details too, such as the statues and the staircase of The Four Times of Day at the western end.

For a phone, try a wide shot first, then move closer for a statue or a stretch of railing. Keep other visitors out of the edges of the frame if you can, or wait a moment for a gap.
text.geographic_location: Brühl's Terrace is in Dresden, on the bank of the Elbe just north of the Neumarkt and the Frauenkirche. The staircase at its west end leads up from Schlossplatz.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is given for this spot. The terrace is just north of the Neumarkt and the Frauenkirche, so head to that area and walk north to the river. The staircase from Schlossplatz at the west end is one way up onto the terrace. The phone icon on the map is about 250 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view along the terrace. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the balustrade and buildings will not fit in, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for statues and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 250 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and let the balustrade run along a diagonal line into the frame. Keep the horizon level and include a statue or a lamp in the foreground for depth. Walk a little way along the terrace for closer shots of the staircase, the statues and the Albertinum.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Portrait mode works well for a person standing at the railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light, and a quieter terrace is easier to photograph. Check the weather, as the open view over the river looks best with some sky.

text.access_note: Brühl's Terrace was opened to the public in 1814. Please check locally for current access before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west from the east end, morning light falls on the building fronts from behind the photographer, while evening light comes from behind the subject.
The terrace is usually busier in the middle of the day.
The Elbe lies on the north side of the terrace, below the balustrade.

name: Fürstenzug
label: Fürstenzug
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stallhof' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Stallhof' (way/163206106): middle (50 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Fürstenzug'.

text.description:
The Fürstenzug, or Procession of Princes, is a long mural of Saxony's rulers on horseback, running along the outer wall of the Stallhof of Dresden Castle. It was first painted between 1871 and 1876 by Wilhelm Walther to mark 800 years of the House of Wettin. The paint wore badly, so between 1904 and 1907 the scene was recreated on about 23,000 Meissen porcelain tiles. The wall is roughly 102 metres long and shows 35 margraves, electors, dukes and kings, from 1127 to 1904, with the name of each ruler written beneath him. Many ordinary people are shown too, such as scientists, craftsmen, children and farmers. Only minimal damage to the tiles came from the bombing of 13 February 1945.

It photographs well because the cream and brown tiles form one continuous band of detail, and the horses and figures give a natural rhythm. The challenge is the length. The street is narrow, so you cannot fit everything in one frame from close by. Treat it as a series: one picture to show the scale, then a few close shots of single riders, faces, horses' heads and the lettering. The courtyard behind the wall is a calmer place to start, with its white arches and columns. Whichever spot you choose, keep your phone steady, avoid flash, and give other visitors room to pass.
text.geographic_location: In Dresden, on the outer wall of the Stallhof of Dresden Castle, facing Augustusstraße. The Hofkirche is reported to be at one end of the mural.
text.directions_text: Head for Dresden Castle, then look for Augustusstraße along the castle's Stallhof wall. Once there, walk to the phone icon on the map, in the Stallhof courtyard. From there the mural is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the arches and columns of the courtyard. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a long stretch of the street in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single riders and tile details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m south-west of the subject, in Stallhof (the phone icon on the map), and face north-east. Inside the courtyard beside the arched colonnade on the rear side of the mural. The white arcades and columns frame the wall of the mural, and this is a quieter, less crowded setting than the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the arches as a natural frame around the wall, keeping the verticals straight. For a detail shot, zoom in on one or two riders and leave the rest out. For the full length of the procession, try the end of the street by the Hofkirche (reported, so confirm on arrival), where the wall runs away from you with the Frauenkirche dome behind. Augustusstraße gives a close-up of the porcelain with the dome above the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the tiles to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the highlights down if the wall is partly in bright sun. Keep the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The wall gets direct sun for only a few minutes a day, so even, bright, overcast light is easiest for exposure.

text.access_note: The mural is on a public street and the Stallhof courtyard is free to enter, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or events.
claims_not_in_sources: Overcast light makes the exposure easier on a wall that is mostly in shade.
The Hofkirche is reported to be at one end of the mural; this placement is inferred from guides' descriptions and should be confirmed on site.

name: Albertinum
label: Albertinum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brühlsche Terrasse' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Brühlsche Terrasse' (relation/3288098): middle (309 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q699780 (coordinate location).

text.description:
The Albertinum is a big sandstone museum of modern art on the eastern end of Brühl's Terrace, in Dresden's historic centre. Its Renaissance Revival front looks solid and handsome, and it makes a good subject because it sits right at the edge of the terrace with the Frauenkirche rising behind it and the Elbe meadows beyond. That gives you a layered scene of old and new Dresden in a single frame.

The building has a long history. An armoury was built on the site between 1559 and 1563. It was extended between 1884 and 1887 to house the royal sculpture collection, and it was named after King Albert of Saxony. It was damaged in the bombing of 13 February 1945 and restored by 1953. After the 2002 floods and a closure in 2006, it reopened on 20 June 2010 with the inner courtyard roofed over to make a glazed atrium. Today it holds the New Masters Gallery and the Sculpture Collection.

For photographs, start on the terrace itself. The small park at the eastern end, above the Kasematten, frames the museum against the Frauenkirche. Take one wide shot to show the whole setting, then step in for a tighter one of the facade's stonework and windows. If you go inside, the atrium is a good second subject for a quieter architectural picture, but check the official site before you go to see what is open to visitors and whether photography is allowed.

text.description:
The Augustus Bridge is the road bridge over the Elbe that links the Innere Neustadt on the north bank with Dresden's historic centre on the south bank. It is a sandstone bridge with nine arches, built between 1907 and 1910 to designs by Wilhelm Kreis and Theodor Klette. It replaced an earlier sandstone bridge with 12 arches, built under Augustus II the Strong between 1727 and 1731. That one was taken down to give river traffic a wider opening. A stone bridge was first built at this location in 1220, so you are photographing a very old crossing point.

It photographs well because the row of arches gives you a strong, repeating shape that leads the eye along the river. Three tram lines also run over it, so a passing tram adds some life and colour to the picture. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m north-east of the subject. That lets you show the whole span rather than only the roadway.

For a phone, keep it simple. Use the default lens (1x) for the bridge and the water, and switch on gridlines so the parapet and the arches stay level. Wait for a tram to cross if you want movement in the frame. Take a few shots, because people and traffic keep moving across the scene.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Elbe in the centre of Dresden, between the Innere Neustadt on the north bank and the historic city centre on the south bank.
text.directions_text: Start from the Innere Neustadt, on the north bank of the Elbe, or from the historic centre on the south bank, and cross towards the river. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit several arches and the river into the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and want the full span. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single arch or a tram on the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the parapet or the tops of the arches up with a horizontal line. Place the bridge on the lower third and leave some sky above. Let the arches and the water lead the eye into the picture. If a tram is approaching, hold the phone ready and take several shots as it crosses.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the sandstone keeps its detail. Switch on Live Photos or motion if you want a little movement from passing trams. Keep your elbows against your body to stay steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light and fewer people on the pavements. After dark, use night mode and brace your phone against a solid surface for a sharper shot.

text.access_note: This is a public road bridge in use by trams and traffic, so keep clear of the tram tracks and traffic; check the official site before you go if you need details of any works or closures.

text.description:
The Golden Rider (Goldener Reiter) is a gilded statue of a figure on horseback, and it stands out as soon as you step into Neustädter Markt in Dresden's Inner Neustadt. The gold is the main reason it works on a phone. Against a plain sky or a muted building it is easy to pick out, so you can build a simple, bold photo around it with very little fuss.

Check the sky behind it before you press the shutter. A bright, empty sky can make your phone darken the picture, so tap on the gold and nudge the exposure slider until the surface shows its colour and detail instead of a flat yellow glare.

If other visitors are around, wait a moment or shoot from slightly lower down and tilt up a little. That keeps most people out of the frame and makes the statue look taller. Keep the gridlines on so the plinth stays level and the buildings don't lean. Take a few frames in both portrait and landscape orientation. The portrait one suits a single statue, and the landscape one gives you the square around it as context.

text.description:
Pfunds Molkerei is a dairy shop on Bautzner Straße in Dresden's Äußere Neustadt. It is best known for the hand-painted tiles that cover its interior, along with the counter and chandeliers. Most visitors come for that interior, and it is the scene guides usually call the classic photo. From the street, though, the shop is a plain facade that gives little hint of what is inside. That makes the pavement opposite the shop, at Bautzner Straße 79, a context shot: it shows the shop in its everyday setting on the street, and it works well as the first picture in a set before you go in.

The shop is closed on Sundays and public holidays, except Advent Sundays. Bus tours stop outside briefly, so the pavement can be busy for a few minutes at a time. If you go inside, the rules say no flash, no tripods and no selfie sticks. Advice on photography indoors is mixed: the shop's website says photos are welcome as long as they do not hinder other guests or staff, while one blog says written permission was needed. Ask a member of staff politely and take your pictures in a quiet moment. From the pavement opposite, use the shop front, the signage and the street around it to tell the story. Stay clear of other people's doorways and keep the pavement free for passers-by.

text.description:
The Kreuzkirche, or Church of the Holy Cross, is a Lutheran church on the edge of Dresden's old market square. It is the largest church building in Saxony and the home of the Dresdner Kreuzchor boys' choir. The church was dedicated to the Holy Cross in 1388, but the building you see today is mostly the work of the late 1700s, after Prussian guns wrecked the earlier church in the Seven Years' War. Fires have damaged it more than once. The last was during the bombing of Dresden on 13 February 1945, and the church reopened in 1955.

It photographs well because the tall tower and plain, broad front stand out against the buildings around the square. Taken from the Altmarkt, the church sits neatly in the frame with the Altstadt buildings on either side, which is why this is the natural postcard position.

For a phone, stay out in the open square. Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the tower and the whole front together. Step back if the top gets cut off. Switch to telephoto for the upper tower, or to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square around you. The Striezelmarkt Christmas market fills the Altmarkt in Advent and can block this view. Pfarrgasse, a narrow lane nearby, is an alternative if you want the church framed at the end of an old-town street. Photography inside the church may be restricted, so ask before taking pictures there.
text.geographic_location: The Kreuzkirche stands in Dresden's Altstadt (old town), on the south-eastern side of the Altmarkt, the old market square, not far from the Frauenkirche.

The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

From here the church is to the south-east, and you see its tower and main front across the open square with the Altstadt buildings framing it on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright against a vertical line. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean inwards, and leave a little sky above the tower top. Let the buildings at the edges act as a frame. For a different view, try Pfarrgasse for the church at the end of a narrow lane, but check on the map first.

text.description:
The Großer Garten is a Baroque park in central Dresden, laid out in 1676 on the orders of John George III, Elector of Saxony. It has been open to the public since 1814. The rectangle covers about 1.8 square kilometres, and its paths and avenues are arranged symmetrically. At the centre stands the Sommerpalais, a small pleasure palace (a Lustschloss). The palace is the subject of this spot.

The best-known view is from the Palaisteich, the pond in front of the palace. Across the still water you see the palace facade and its reflection, framed by trees, which makes a tidy, balanced picture even for a first-time visitor.

Stand on the south-east shore and look west towards the palace. Keep the palace roughly central and let the trees close in on both sides. If you want something more symmetrical, the Hauptallee, the long tree-lined main avenue, leads the eye straight to the palace. The park is big, so wear comfortable shoes and allow time to wander. Evening is the time to aim for, when the palace is lit up and the pond picks up the glow. Check the official site before you go if you want to see inside the palace, as the building itself may have its own visiting arrangements.
text.geographic_location: In central Dresden, at the heart of the Großer Garten park. The palace sits at the middle of the park, and the Palaisteich pond lies in front of it.

Once you are in the park, make for the Palaisteich pond in front of the palace. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the palace along the centre or a third line, with the water filling the lower part so the reflection is included. Keep the phone level so the facade does not lean. For a different view, try the Hauptallee, where the palace closes the long avenue in a symmetrical shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the facade does not wash out and the reflection stays rich. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing. Take a few shots in case ripples blur the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the palace is illuminated and its reflection glows on the pond.

text.description:
Neumarkt is the square around the Frauenkirche in the heart of Dresden's old town. It began as a small settlement on a slight rise above the Elbe, and when the city walls were extended in 1530 it became the 'New Market', the second market square alongside the Altmarkt. Under August II the Strong the square was lined with baroque buildings, and today's houses are mostly reconstructions of them. The area was almost completely destroyed in the firestorm of February 1945. The Frauenkirche was finished again in 2005, and the streets around it have since been rebuilt in stages, mostly to the original structure or with facades close to the old ones.

That history is why it photographs so well. The dome rises above rows of tall burgher-style houses, which close in around it like a frame. The classic picture is taken from the middle of the square, facing east, with the church filling the frame and the houses on either side. Go early in the morning if you can, when the square is empty and you can shoot without people crossing the view. There has been construction work near the square, so look for scaffolding before you set up. If you want a second angle, the Brühlsche Terrasse gives a view down the Münzgasse with the dome at the end of the lane, and Rampische Straße shows the church at the end of the street between old facades.
text.geographic_location: Neumarkt lies in the old town (Altstadt) of central Dresden, on the square that surrounds the Frauenkirche. It is the old town's second market square, alongside the Altmarkt.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Frauenkirche in the old town, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further out. Neumarkt is the square around the church. Once you are in the square, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of it, and Neumarkt itself is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the dome and the houses on both sides in a natural-looking frame. If you want the whole dome and more of the rooftops, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). If you want to pick out the dome or a single facade, use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m south-east of the subject, in Neumarkt (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. From there the dome sits in the centre, with the baroque burgher houses framing the square on either side. Neumarkt itself is a little to the north-west of where you are standing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the centre line, with the houses balanced left and right. Keep your phone level so the facades do not lean. For a different angle, try the view down the Münzgasse from the Brühlsche Terrasse, where the dome appears at the end of the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework of the church to set focus and exposure, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few frames at 1x and 0.5x so you can pick the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is empty.

text.access_note: Neumarkt is a public square. There is construction near the square, so check for scaffolding and any closures before you go, and look at the official Frauenkirche site if you plan to go inside.

text.description: The Japanese Palace is a Baroque building on the Neustadt side of the Elbe, with a garden around it. It photographs well because of its large, formal shape and the greenery in front, which gives you a natural foreground for a phone shot. The palace dates from 1715. Between 1729 and 1731 it was extended so that Augustus the Strong could display his Japanese porcelain there, although that plan was never carried out and it later served as the Saxon Library. It was designed by Pöppelmann, Longuelune and de Bodt. The building was damaged in the bombing raids of 13 February 1945, and much of the palace and its gardens was restored by the French government, finishing in the 1980s. Today it houses three museums: the Museum of Ethnology Dresden, the State Museum for Pre-History and the Senckenberg Natural History Collection. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m south-west of the subject. From there you can fit the building and some of the garden into one frame without needing to go inside. Turn on gridlines so the roofline and walls sit straight. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then a closer zoomed shot of the facade. Before you go, look at the official site to see which parts of the grounds you can enter.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't look washed out. If you zoom to 3x or more, hold the phone with both hands and take a couple of shots to be sure one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame. On a bright midday the sky can overpower the building, so use the exposure slider.

text.access_note: The palace houses museums and the garden may have its own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Yenidze
label: Yenidze
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brühlsche Terrasse' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Brühlsche Terrasse' (relation/3288098): middle (309 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Yenidze'.

text.description:
The Yenidze is a former cigarette factory that looks like a mosque, which is exactly why people stop to photograph it. It was built between 1907 and 1909 for a tobacco company, and its Moorish Revival design was meant to recall the eastern origins of the tobacco and to work as advertising. The architect was Martin Hammitzsch. Colourful tilework, about 600 windows of different styles and a dome 20 metres high give the building plenty of detail. The chimneys are dressed up like minarets, but it was never a mosque. It came through the bombing of February 1945 relatively unharmed, apart from some coloured glass lost from the dome. It then stood almost alone for decades until the area was rebuilt. It was restored in 1996 and is now used as offices.

The dome and chimney rise above the nearby roofs, and the best moment is dusk, when the dome is lit. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the wider ones show the riverside setting and the closer ones show the dome shape. If you have time, the Marienbrücke is a good second spot, showing the dome and chimney above the railway tracks.
text.geographic_location: The viewpoint, the Brühlsche Terrasse, is on the riverside in the Altstadt.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Altstadt and reach the Brühlsche Terrasse on foot, or by taxi or hired scooter. The phone icon on the map is about 1.1 km south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the dome and chimney closer. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider frame that includes the river and the sky. Leave the ultra-wide (0.5x) for other spots, because the Yenidze would look tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.1 km south-east of the subject, on Brühlsche Terrasse (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. At the Elbe-bank end facing the Neustadt side. From here the Yenidze is seen across the Elbe to the north-west, with its dome rising above the river view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the dome on one of the upper intersections, leaving some sky above it. Keep the horizon level and use the river or the bank as a foreground line. If you want a different angle, the Marienbrücke shows the dome and chimney above the railway tracks.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit dome keeps its colour against the darker sky. At dusk, turn on night mode and rest your elbows on the parapet to keep the phone steady. Telephoto shots lose sharpness in low light, so take several and keep the best one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the dome is lit. Aim for the half hour after sunset so the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The Brühlsche Terrasse is an open public promenade, but access near the Carolabrücke end may be affected by the bridge collapse in 2024, so check current access on the day; the Yenidze itself is an office building with a restaurant, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Canaletto view from the Neustadt bank
label: Canaletto view
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).

notes: The skyline Canaletto painted, across the Elbe.

text.description:
Canaletto view from the Neustadt bank is a riverside viewpoint on the Elberadweg, the riverside path in Dresden's Innere Neustadt. The spot is called Canaletto-Blick (Canaletto view). The path runs along the water, so you can walk a few steps either way and try different angles. The river in the foreground gives the picture a natural frame, and the far bank gives you buildings to work with.

The spot is easy to photograph on a phone. Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, with the river at the bottom and the far bank across the middle. Switch on the gridlines so the horizon stays level. If you want more sky or the path in the foreground, try the ultra-wide (0.5x). To pick out individual buildings on the far bank, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone). Ideally, take a few frames at each setting, because the view changes a lot with the zoom. Walkers and cyclists use the path, so wait a moment for a clear gap, and keep your elbows in so you don't block them.
text.geographic_location: On the Neustadt side of the Elbe, on the Elberadweg in Dresden's Innere Neustadt, right by the river.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so plan your own route to the Innere Neustadt riverbank on the north bank of the Elbe and head for the riverside path (Elberadweg). The phone icon on the map is about 140 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more foreground and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single buildings on the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, so the far bank and sky fill most of the picture. Keep the phone level, because tilting it makes the buildings lean. Try one wide shot with the river in the foreground and one tighter shot with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the far bank to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. In dim light, night mode helps, but brace your elbows against your body and hold your breath for a steady shot. Panorama works if you move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening is usually the most flattering time for a riverside view like this. Choose a clear day and check where the sun is before you set up.

text.access_note: This is a riverside path in a public area, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or works on the path.

name: Elbe paddle steamers at the Terrassenufer
label: Paddle steamers
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap: Terrassenufer, Wilsdruffer Vorstadt/Seevorstadt-West, Seevorstadt, Altstadt, Dresden, Sach

text.description:
The paddle steamers at the Terrassenufer are one of the classic Elbe scenes in Dresden's Altstadt. The paddle steamers are found at the Terrassenufer on the Elbe, and with their tall funnels and broad paddle boxes they make a strong, easy-to-read subject. The long, open riverside also gives you space to step back and fit a whole boat into the frame, with the water in front and the city behind.

Seen from this distance the boats sit nicely among the riverbank, the water and the sky, rather than filling the frame. That gives a calm, postcard-style picture. If you want more detail on a funnel or the paddle wheel, use the telephoto lens and keep your arms steady.

You can also walk closer for a second shot. Low down by the water's edge, the reflections on the water add interest, and a passing boat or a walker gives the picture some scale. The exact boats and their positions can change from day to day, so take whatever is there and build your frame around it.
text.geographic_location: The Terrassenufer runs along the Elbe in Dresden's Altstadt, in the Seevorstadt area on the edge of the old town centre.
text.directions_text: Head for the Terrassenufer on the Elbe in Dresden's Altstadt. The phone icon on the map is about 260 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole riverside scene. Then try the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the boats closer from 265 m away. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to a boat and want it all in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 260 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The paddle steamers sit at the far end of the view. Walk a few steps closer if you want them larger in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the river along the lower third, with the boat on one of the side lines and a good amount of sky above. Keep the horizon level. Hold the phone low for reflections on the water. At 2x or 3x, fill the frame with a funnel and paddle box for a tighter shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boat to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. For a shot with movement, try a Live Photo if a boat happens to be moving. Hold your phone with both hands when zoomed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun is behind you as you look west, tends to light the boats more evenly. Evening can give warm colour in the sky, though the boats may then appear darker against it.

text.access_note: No access information is available for this spot.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west from the stand-here point, morning sun is behind the photographer and lights the boats more evenly.
In the evening the sun is in the west, so the boats may appear darker against the sky when looking that way.
The boats' positions and which boats are present can change from day to day.
